parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Stanhope Bathrooms**
> 
> Stanhope Bathrooms sells bathroom fittings in country R through showrooms and online. Until now, the showroom team, the online team and the advertising agency have each set their own prices, promotions and product photography.
> 
> The same tap is priced at \$95 online and \$128 in showrooms, and a discount advertised on television last month was not available in showrooms. Customer complaints have risen by 40%.

Analyse **two** benefits to Stanhope Bathrooms of adopting a coordinated marketing strategy.
parts.solution_md:
A coordinated marketing strategy is one in which the elements of the marketing mix are planned together so they support the same objective **[K]**. At present the same tap sells for \$95 online and \$128 in showrooms **[Ap]**. Coordinating pricing would either set one price across both channels or make the difference explicable, which matters because a customer who finds the same product \$33 cheaper elsewhere in the same business concludes they have been overcharged **[An]**. That perception is a likely cause of the 40% rise in complaints, and complaints both absorb staff time and deter the repeat and word-of-mouth business that showrooms rely on **[An]** Coordination would also align promotion with what the channels can actually offer **[K]**. The discount advertised on television last month was not available in showrooms **[Ap]**. Planning promotion and channel together would ensure an advertised offer can be honoured wherever the customer chooses to buy **[An]**. At the moment Stanhope Bathrooms pays for television advertising that draws customers into showrooms only to disappoint them, so its advertising spending is generating complaints rather than sales; coordinating the two would convert the same budget into completed purchases **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Ledbury Print**
> 
> Ledbury Print provides commercial printing in country F. It has repositioned itself as a fast-turnaround service, promising delivery within 48 hours, and its advertising emphasises speed.
> 
> However, its website quotes a standard lead time of seven days, its sales team offers discounts to customers who place orders four weeks in advance, and its two largest presses are 15 years old and break down roughly twice a month.

Analyse **two** problems that a lack of consistency in Ledbury Print's marketing strategy may cause.
parts.solution_md:
A marketing strategy is consistent when the promise made to customers matches what the business actually delivers **[K]**. Ledbury Print advertises 48-hour delivery, yet its website quotes seven days and its main presses break down about twice a month **[Ap]**. Customers attracted by the speed claim will therefore find it is not met, and in commercial printing, where work is usually placed under deadline, a missed delivery causes the customer real disruption **[An]**. Because printing is bought through repeat contracts rather than one-off purchases, a single failure risks losing all that customer's future orders, not just the one job **[An]** A second problem is that Ledbury Print's own activities contradict one another **[K]**. Its sales team discounts orders placed four weeks ahead, which rewards precisely the long lead times the advertising is designed to move customers away from **[Ap]**. The advertising therefore pulls customers towards urgent work while the pricing pulls them towards planning ahead, so the two cancel out **[An]**. Ledbury Print ends up paying for advertising that attracts urgent orders and then discounting away the premium that fast turnaround should earn, leaving it with the cost of the repositioning but not the benefit **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

> **[case-study]**
> **Carrow**
> 
> Carrow manufactures luggage in country J. Its marketing objective for the next two years is to raise the share of its sales coming from customers aged under 30 from 12% to 25%.
> 
> Its promotion is currently placed in airline magazines and on airport advertising boards. Its range consists mainly of large hard-shell suitcases priced between \$180 and \$260. Research shows that travellers under 30 mostly take short trips with cabin-sized bags and book through mobile apps.

Analyse **two** changes Carrow could make to its marketing strategy in order to achieve this objective.
parts.solution_md:
A marketing strategy should be developed to achieve specific marketing objectives rather than set independently of them **[K]**. Carrow's range is mainly large hard-shell suitcases at \$180 to \$260, while research shows under-30 travellers take short trips with cabin-sized bags **[Ap]**. Introducing a cabin-sized range at a lower price would give the target group a product that matches how they actually travel **[An]**. Without that, any promotion aimed at under-30s would generate interest Carrow could not convert, because the customer would arrive to find nothing suitable in the range **[An]** A second change concerns where Carrow promotes **[K]**. Its promotion currently appears in airline magazines and on airport boards, which reach travellers who have already booked and paid **[Ap]**. Under-30s book through mobile apps, so digital and social channels would reach them at the point where the trip, and the luggage need, is being decided **[An]**. Moving spending to those channels would put the same budget in front of the target segment at the moment the purchase decision is forming, raising the proportion of promotional spending that reaches the customers the objective is about **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

> 
> Pennine Crafts sells craft supplies online in country D. It has 180 000 registered customers and records every product viewed, added to a basket and purchased. It stocks 9 000 different products.
> 
> Its weekly email newsletter goes to every customer with identical content, and the proportion of customers opening it has fallen from 24% to 11% over two years.

Pennine Crafts records every product viewed, basketed and bought by 180 000 customers across 9 000 products **[Ap]**. AI could tailor each newsletter to the craft a customer actually buys for, so a customer who buys wool sees wool products rather than the same general email as everyone else **[An]**. > **[case-study]**
> **Brightside Tyres**
> 
> Brightside Tyres operates 40 tyre-fitting centres in country Q and wants to expand into country M. It is considering franchising: local businesspeople would run centres under the Brightside Tyres name, paying an initial fee and a share of revenue, and buying tyres from Brightside Tyres.
> 
> Brightside Tyres has limited capital. Country M has different vehicle safety regulations from country Q, and an established chain there already operates 120 centres.

Analyse **two** benefits to Brightside Tyres of using franchising to enter the market in country M.
parts.solution_md:
Franchising allows a business to expand by letting others trade under its name in return for a fee and a share of revenue **[K]**. The franchisees, not Brightside Tyres, fund the cost of opening and equipping each centre **[Ap]**. Because Brightside Tyres has limited capital, this lets it enter country M without borrowing heavily or diverting funds from its 40 existing centres **[An]**. It can therefore open more centres, more quickly, than its own finances would allow, which matters when a rival already operates 120 centres and is likely to defend its position **[An]** A second benefit is that franchisees bring local knowledge **[K]**. Country M has different vehicle safety regulations from country Q **[Ap]**. Local franchisees are far more likely to understand those regulations and to know how customers choose a fitting centre, so Brightside Tyres reduces the risk of breaching rules it does not fully understand **[An]**. Avoiding that risk protects the brand at the point of entry, because a safety failure in a new market would damage the reputation Brightside Tyres is relying on to persuade customers to leave the established chain **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Everdon Games**
> 
> Everdon Games publishes board games in country S. In January it produced a detailed marketing plan for the year, setting out promotional spending quarter by quarter and a launch date of October for its main new game.
> 
> In March, a competitor announced a very similar game for release in June, and the cost of printed cardboard rose by 20%.

Explain **one** limitation of marketing planning for Everdon Games.
parts.solution_md:
Marketing planning involves setting out marketing objectives and the actions needed to achieve them in advance **[1]**. Everdon Games wrote its plan in January, but by March a competitor had announced a similar game for June release and cardboard costs had risen by 20% **[1]**. A plan can only reflect the conditions expected when it was written, so keeping to the original October launch would let the competitor reach the market four months earlier, while the promotional budget set in January would no longer cover Everdon Games' higher costs **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Marketing planning sets out objectives and the actions, resources and marketing mix needed to achieve them, decided in advance
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The plan was written in January and could not anticipate the competitor's June release announced in March
> - A fixed October launch date would leave Everdon Games four months behind a very similar rival product
> - Promotional spending set quarter by quarter no longer reflects costs after a 20% rise in cardboard prices
> - Following a plan too rigidly can prevent a business responding to change, while abandoning it removes the benefit of having planned at all
> - Preparing a detailed annual plan takes management time, which is wasted if conditions change soon after it is written
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A limitation is not an argument against doing the thing at all. The examiner wants to see where marketing planning falls short, not a claim that Everdon Games should stop planning. Show the specific point at which the plan stops helping, here the moment its assumptions were overtaken, and you have identified a limitation rather than simply objecting to planning.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Thornbury Paints**
> 
> Thornbury Paints manufactures paint in country W and wants to sell in country B. Paint is heavy and expensive to transport, and country B applies a 25% import tariff on manufactured goods. Thornbury Paints has limited capital and no knowledge of country B's regulations on chemical products.

Explain **one** factor that may influence the method Thornbury Paints uses to enter country B.
parts.solution_md:
Methods of entering an international market include exporting, licensing, joint ventures and setting up production overseas **[1]**. Paint is heavy to transport and country B charges a 25% import tariff on manufactured goods **[1]**. Both raise the delivered cost of exporting from country W, so Thornbury Paints may find a joint venture or licensing arrangement with a producer inside country B more viable, since producing locally avoids both the tariff and the freight cost, and a local partner would already understand country B's chemical regulations **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Methods of entry include exporting, licensing, franchising, joint ventures and direct investment in overseas production
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The 25% tariff makes exporting expensive, favouring a method that involves producing inside country B
> - Paint is heavy relative to its value, so transport costs reinforce the case against exporting
> - Limited capital makes licensing or a joint venture more realistic than building a factory
> - No knowledge of country B's chemical regulations makes a local partner valuable, since compliance failures could stop sales entirely
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read carefully whether the question asks whether to enter a market or how to enter it. This one asks about the method, so arguments about whether country B is worth entering at all score nothing, however well made. Once you have spotted that, use the case details to push towards one method rather than another.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Redmoor**
> 
> Redmoor is a parcel delivery business in country T, considering expansion into one of two neighbouring countries.
> 
> Country J has a large population and fast-growing online shopping, but poor roads and no address system in rural areas. Country K is smaller and growing slowly, but has reliable roads and an established postal address system.

Explain **one** factor Redmoor should consider when selecting which international market to enter.
parts.solution_md:
Selecting an international market involves comparing possible countries against criteria such as market size, growth and how easily the business can operate there **[1]**. Country J has a large population and fast-growing online shopping, but poor roads and no address system in rural areas **[1]**. For a parcel delivery business, being able to locate an address and reach it is essential, so the country offering the larger opportunity may be the one Redmoor is least able to serve, and failed deliveries would raise its costs and damage its reputation with retailers **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Selecting an international market means assessing possible countries against criteria such as size, growth, competition and ease of operating there
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Country J's poor roads and missing rural addresses directly obstruct the service Redmoor sells, whatever the size of the market
> - Country K's reliable roads and address system would allow Redmoor to operate its existing model with little change
> - Fast-growing online shopping in country J represents genuine long-term potential if the delivery obstacles could be overcome
> - Failed deliveries damage relationships with the retailers who provide the parcels, not only with the end customer
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Selecting a market means rejecting one, so a strong answer says what would rule a country out, not only what makes one attractive. Here the larger, faster-growing market is also the harder one to serve. Showing that the two criteria point in opposite directions is what lifts an answer above simply listing what a business "should think about".

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Ivybridge Cards**
> 
> Ivybridge Cards designs and prints greeting cards in country M. Its home market is small and sales have been flat for two years. Around 70% of its cards carry no written message, only images.

Explain **one** reason why international marketing may be important for Ivybridge Cards.
parts.solution_md:
International marketing means promoting and selling a product in markets outside a business's home country **[1]**. Ivybridge Cards operates in a small home market where sales have been flat for two years **[1]**. Because 70% of its cards carry images rather than written messages, they would need little adaptation to sell abroad, so overseas markets offer Ivybridge Cards a route to the growth its home market can no longer provide, and without the cost of redesigning most of its range **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - International marketing is the promotion and sale of products in markets outside the business's home country
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The home market is small and sales have been flat for two years, so growth must come from elsewhere
> - Cards carrying images rather than text need little translation or redesign, lowering the cost of entering new markets
> - Selling in several countries would reduce dependence on one small market and the risk that comes with it
> - Higher volumes across more markets could reduce printing costs per card through economies of scale
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Importance" questions are always importance to the named business, never importance in general. Anyone can write that international marketing increases sales. The marks come from why it matters to this firm in this situation, so anchor your answer in the flat home sales and the fact that most of the cards carry no words.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Vanta Telecom**
> 
> Vanta Telecom provides mobile phone services in country F. It holds records of how much data each of its 2 million customers uses, when they contact customer service, and which tariffs they have changed. Until now it has sent the same promotional offer to every customer.

Explain **one** way in which information technology could improve Vanta Telecom's marketing.
parts.solution_md:
Information technology allows a business to collect, store and analyse large amounts of customer data **[1]**. Vanta Telecom already holds records of data use, service contacts and tariff changes for 2 million customers **[1]**. Analysing these records would let it identify which customers show signs of leaving, such as repeated service complaints, and send those customers a targeted offer rather than the same offer to everyone, retaining more customers for the same promotional spending **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Information technology enables a business to collect, store and analyse customer data to inform marketing decisions
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Records of data use and tariff changes allow Vanta Telecom to group customers and target offers rather than promoting to all 2 million identically
> - Patterns in customer service contacts could identify customers at risk of leaving, so retention offers can be directed where they matter
> - Targeted promotion reduces waste, so the same marketing budget generates more response
> - Usage data could reveal demand for tariffs Vanta Telecom does not yet offer, informing product decisions as well as promotion
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Marks for technology questions sit in what the technology changes, not in what it is. Describing the systems a business owns is background; the examiner wants the decision it can now make that it could not make before. Move quickly from "it holds data" to "so it can do this specific thing differently".

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Wensley**
> 
> Wensley produces handmade artisan cheese in country D. It sells through delicatessens at premium prices, and its brand is built on traditional methods. Wensley has been offered shelf space by a discount supermarket chain, which would require it to cut its price by 40% and use plain packaging.

Explain **one** reason why Wensley's marketing strategy should be consistent with its product and its market.
parts.solution_md:
A marketing strategy is consistent when the product, price, promotion and place all match one another and suit the customers being targeted **[1]**. Wensley sells handmade cheese at premium prices through delicatessens, and its brand rests on traditional methods **[1]**. Selling the same cheese at a 40% lower price in plain packaging through a discount chain would contradict that positioning, and customers currently paying a premium may conclude the product was never worth it, damaging the delicatessen sales Wensley depends on **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A consistent marketing strategy is one in which the elements of the mix match the nature of the product and the market it is aimed at
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A 40% price cut contradicts a premium positioning built on handmade, traditional production
> - Plain packaging removes the visual signals customers use to justify paying more
> - Existing delicatessen customers may switch to the cheaper outlet or lose confidence in the brand entirely
> - Delicatessens may drop Wensley if the same cheese appears at a much lower price elsewhere, costing it its established route to market
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Consistent" is a relationship, so it always needs a second half. An answer saying Wensley's strategy "should be consistent" without naming what it must be consistent with has not yet said anything. State both sides: the premium, handmade product on one hand and the discount, plain-packaged offer on the other, and the contradiction does the analytical work for you.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Hartley Instruments**
> 
> Hartley Instruments makes guitars and violins in country R. It has never written a marketing plan, and decisions about promotion are taken by the owner month by month. Sales have grown, but the marketing budget was overspent by 30% last year.

Explain **one** benefit to Hartley Instruments of producing a marketing plan.
parts.solution_md:
A marketing plan sets out a business's marketing objectives and the actions needed to achieve them **[1]**. Hartley Instruments currently makes promotional decisions month by month and overspent its marketing budget by 30% last year **[1]**. A plan would set out spending for the whole year in advance and link it to agreed objectives, so the owner could see when spending was running ahead of target and correct it during the year rather than discovering the overspend once it had already happened **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A marketing plan sets out marketing objectives and the actions, resources and marketing mix needed to achieve them
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Planned annual spending would allow the 30% overspend to be spotted and corrected during the year rather than after it
> - Month-by-month decisions leave no way of judging whether promotion is working; a plan gives objectives to measure against
> - A plan would coordinate promotion across guitars and violins rather than treating each decision separately
> - Written objectives make it easier to justify marketing spending as the business grows and more people become involved in decisions
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Where a spec point covers two halves, benefits and limitations, check which half the question wants before you write. A well-argued limitation earns nothing on a question asking for a benefit. Underline the key word in the stem, then make sure every sentence you write serves that word.

Pan-global marketing is a strategy in which a business uses the same marketing mix in every country where it sells **[1]**, rather than adapting its product, price or promotion to suit local tastes **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
>

Evaluate **two **changes that UBH could make to its current marketing strategy to increase sales and reach its target capacity utilisation.
parts.solution_md:
One change UBH could make is to increase its use of informative social media promotion **[K]** specifically targeting business start-ups. Market research shows that most new start-ups are unaware of the benefits of co-working, yet this group is exactly the type of customer UBH has always targeted  **[Ap]**. Social media advertising is already UBH's most cost-effective marketing method, meaning that increasing the budget for targeted campaigns is likely to produce a strong return **[An]**. These campaigns should focus on educating potential customers about what co-working offers - flexible contracts, internet access, printing, and meeting rooms - rather than simply promoting UBH's brand. Raising awareness among this previously unreached segment could increase demand significantly and help UBH move from 80% to its target of 100% capacity utilisation **[Ap]** **[An]**

A second change is to develop premium facilities in selected beehives **[K]** to attract large businesses and multinationals. Market research shows that some larger businesses use co-working centres but demand higher specification facilities **[Ap]**. These customers would generate significantly higher revenue per booking than small businesses or start-ups **[An]**. However, this change carries risks - premium facilities require more space per desk, which would reduce the total number of desks available and potentially lower overall capacity utilisation in those beehives unless the higher revenue compensates **[An]**

Overall, the most effective change is the social media promotion strategy **[E]**, because it directly addresses an identified gap - start-up unawareness - at relatively low cost and builds on a method already proven to work for UBH **[Ap]**. The premium facilities option could complement this in the longer term, but needs significant capital investment at a time when UBH is already planning major expansion **[Ap]**. UBH should prioritise promotion first, and consider targeted premium development once its expansion plans are more established and cash flow is stronger **[E]**

Interest rates are very low as the monetary policy of these countries is aiming to boost demand. However, this has contributed to exchange rate depreciations of the US dollar and the European euro. Consumer spending has fallen due to declining real incomes. There are ageing populations in most of the countries where PC sells its products. A loss of competitiveness in many industrial sectors has resulted in rising unemployment. Statement of financial position valuations Since 2008 PC’s share price has fallen. This has been the trend for many public limited companies. PC’s Finance Director has been considering three changes that will affect PC’s accounts. He could make all three changes or just one or two of them. • When calculating depreciation of new production equipment bought last year for \$25m, use an estimated life of 8 years not 5 years. I think we should develop a range of soft drinks to suit local tastes with brand names that reflect local language and culture. We could distribute these new drinks through small retail stores and street markets. This way we will slowly but steadily build up consumer awareness and loyalty.’
